body.x: A strawberry farm changes every day. The position, size and ripeness of the fruit shift, leaves and stems hide berries, and the fruit itself is soft enough to bruise at a clumsy touch. Those conditions make harvesting hard to automate, and farms in many countries are short of workers for it.

Beyond Robotics Co., Ltd., a Physical AI robotics company in Geumcheon-gu, Seoul, has chosen that setting for its first product. Led by CEO Sungho Byun, the company received an Innovation Award at the FIX 2026 Innovation Awards, and its application says it will attend the awards ceremony.

According to the company, Beyond Robotics was established to address labor shortages and repetitive, physically demanding work in industries such as agriculture and food and beverage, which it describes as some of the most challenging unstructured environments for automation. Byun holds bachelor's and master's degrees in mechanical engineering from Korea University and previously worked at LG Electronics' Production Engineering Research Institute and the AI robotics company CMES Robotics, where he developed 3D vision and robotic automation solutions. COO Younghoon Jeong holds a bachelor of business in marketing from the University of Newcastle in Australia, worked on business and marketing strategy and product planning at an LG Electronics division and at the KAON Group's corporate planning office, and later served as head of marketing at CMES Robotics, where he gained experience in commercializing AI robotics and in the company's initial public offering (IPO). In his own description, Byun solves repetitive, physically demanding work in the real world with Physical AI robots that perceive, decide and act on their own in places like agriculture and food and beverage, where labor shortages are severe and conventional automation is hard to implement.

The company says its Physical AI approach joins AI vision, robotic manipulation, autonomous navigation, task planning and control in one system, so that robots can work in settings where the location and shape of objects keep changing and where living organisms call for delicate, hygienic handling. Its first commercial product is PICKY, an autonomous strawberry harvesting robot. Beyond Robotics says a 3D vision system mounted at the end of the robot's arm views strawberries and their surroundings from several angles as the arm moves, and AI identifies harvestable fruit, plans the arm's motion and task sequence, and harvests with a purpose-built end effector. Because strawberries are soft and easily damaged, the company says PICKY cuts the stem instead of gripping the fruit, which it says improves hygiene and minimizes damage.

The robot has a dual-arm configuration to raise productivity, and the company says the two arms work while taking account of the surrounding crops and each other's working areas. In real-world field environments, Beyond Robotics reports a harvesting success rate of about 95%, a maximum harvesting rate of 14 to 16 strawberries per minute and a fruit loss rate below 1%. PICKY also performs initial sorting by size and transportation. According to the company, it navigates growing facilities on its own, decides harvesting areas and task sequences, and can run unmanned harvesting during the day and at night, and it can work with PICKY HUB, which automatically replaces full strawberry trays so operation can continue with less human intervention.

On its field record, Beyond Robotics says PICKY has been operated at multiple commercial smart farms since 2025 and tested at farms, agricultural research institutes and smart farm innovation facilities. At BerryRice, a smart farm in Gimje, Jeollabuk-do, it has been deployed in an actual strawberry-growing environment. In June 2026, the company signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Gyeongsangbuk-do Agricultural Research & Extension Services for the validation, deployment and commercialization of strawberry harvesting robots, and it is working toward wider commercial deployment in 2027. It has a written purchase commitment for one PICKY unit in the first quarter of 2027, and was selected as a resident company at the Gimje Smart Farm Innovation Valley, where it runs its own field-testing site. It has demonstrated PICKY at a summer-strawberry smart farm in Gangneung and an indoor farm in Daegu, with deployment and commercial contracts under discussion, and is talking with other domestic smart farm operators, growers and agricultural organizations about sales and rental-based deployments. The company says letters of intent (LOIs) for adoption exceed KRW 1.2 billion in cumulative value.

It was selected for the Private Excellent Technology Commercialization Support Program and the TIPS program in 2024. In 2026, it filed eight patent applications covering 3D vision, robot control, autonomous harvesting and agricultural task automation, five of which have been registered or received decisions to register. Its main customers, the company says, are smart farm operators and commercial growers in Korea and abroad that cultivate strawberries and other fruit and vegetables at scale, along with public and agricultural organizations such as agricultural research institutes, agricultural technology centers and smart farm innovation valleys.

Beyond Robotics has not exported yet. It says it is receiving inquiries from companies and investment organizations in the Netherlands, Spain, Japan, China and Australia and is discussing possible business and partnership opportunities. It lists Europe, especially the Netherlands, along with North America, Australia and Japan as key target markets, citing developed smart farming and greenhouse horticulture industries, labor shortages and high labor costs. It plans to validate PICKY across different cultivation methods and facility structures with local smart farm operators and agricultural companies, then move through field demonstrations and PoCs toward commercial deployment and exports.

The company's main difficulty is regulatory. Autonomous harvesting robots are an emerging product category with limited commercial deployment worldwide, and it says the certification, inspection, testing standards and related frameworks needed for export and field deployment have not been fully established, which creates uncertainty in preparing for overseas entry and product validation. It says timely international standardization of regulatory, testing and certification frameworks for agricultural Physical AI robots would help Korean companies enter global markets faster.

Its plan is to launch PICKY officially in January 2027 and expand sales to smart farms and agricultural organizations in Korea, standardizing the robot for different cultivation methods and facility structures. In the medium to long term, it intends to extend PICKY from harvesting to crop monitoring, spraying and leaf removal, validate it on tomatoes, cherry tomatoes, cucumbers and bell peppers, and take its Physical AI solutions into unstructured environments in food and beverage, retail and logistics.

FIX 2026 is the third edition of a future-industry exhibition that links innovative technologies in future mobility, robotics, AI and ICT, and startups. It will run from Wednesday, Oct. 21, to Saturday, Oct. 24, at EXCO in Daegu. Under the theme "AI, Beyond Tech into Reality," it offers AI-based technology exhibitions, conferences and lectures by experts from Korea and abroad, and networking programs that share industry trends and core technologies.
